strengths: The empirical gains at 80–90% unstructured sparsity are unusually large and consistent across six model/scale settings, suggesting a potentially important direction beyond layer-wise reconstruction pruning.
The method is conceptually clear: globally optimize the next-token objective with ADMM, add an empirical-Fisher-aware projection, and use low-precision auxiliary states for scaling.
The evaluation covers OPT, Gemma, and LLaMA models from 125M to 27B, two perplexity datasets, seven zero-shot tasks, and multiple sparsity patterns.
The appendix provides numerical results, hardware information, training settings, and many sparsity-specific hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central comparison is confounded by data and compute. Baselines use 128 calibration sequences, while ELSA performs 4,096 full-model optimization steps with batch size 8 and a much larger dataset. Without equally trained, compute-matched baselines or standard sparse-retraining controls, the results do not establish that ADMM—rather than extensive retraining—causes the gains.

The convergence proof contains a serious error: it states that S={x: ||x||_0<=k} is finite and uses this to make the projected iterate eventually constant along a subsequence. This set is infinite, invalidating a key step of Theorem A.4 as written.

The analyzed algorithm does not clearly match ELSA-L as implemented. It changes dual-variable conventions, does not faithfully model quantization of both auxiliary states, omits the Fisher-aware projection, and assumes an approximate x-update condition that is not connected to Adam/adam8bit. The theory therefore does not substantiate the implemented method.

Claims of preserving high fidelity are overstated. At 90% sparsity, LLaMA-2-7B changes from 7.26 to 23.14 C4 perplexity and from 59.67% to 38.52% average zero-shot accuracy. These are strong relative results but substantial absolute degradation. ELSA also often trails existing methods at 50–60% sparsity and under N:M sparsity.

The ablations do not isolate the contribution: there is no compute/data-matched NTP-versus-reconstruction comparison, ordinary masked-training control, ADMM-versus-non-ADMM comparison, convergence study, or adequate sensitivity analysis for training steps and penalty schedules.

Practical efficiency is not demonstrated through wall-clock time, GPU-hours, FLOPs, absolute peak memory, inference latency, or throughput. The claimed 66% memory reduction is not supported by measured results, and unstructured sparsity alone does not imply deployment speedups.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code and environment links are blank, exact main-experiment training-set sizes and data protocols are unclear, and seeds, variance, stopping criteria, and several optimizer/projection details are missing.

The 27B evidence comprises only one model and sparsity level, omits methods deemed infeasible without measured resource comparisons, and reports only perplexity, providing limited support for the broad scalability claim.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and reports striking improvements at 80–90% unstructured sparsity across six model configurations spanning 125M to 13B parameters.
The evaluation includes perplexity, seven zero-shot tasks, multiple sparsity patterns, several recent baselines, and an additional 27B low-precision experiment.
Optimizing the language-modeling objective globally instead of independently reconstructing layers is intuitive, and the objective-aware projection ablation indicates a potentially useful component.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and extensive numerical results are included in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central comparison is substantially confounded by unequal data and compute. Baselines use the conventional 128 calibration sequences, whereas ELSA performs 4,096 Adam steps with batch size 8 and a larger, unspecified dataset—32,768 sequence slots, potentially about 256 times the baseline data exposure. No baseline receives comparable fine-tuning data or optimization compute, so the experiments do not establish that the gains arise from the proposed ADMM formulation rather than extensive task-objective retraining.

Training cost, wall-clock time, GPU-hours, and end-to-end memory are not compared. ELSA uses multiple A100/H200 GPUs and full-precision optimizer states for most experiments, while several baselines are inexpensive one-shot methods. Consequently, the claimed efficiency and practical advantage are inadequately supported.

The convergence proof contains a serious error: it explicitly argues that the l0 constraint set S is finite, but S={x: ||x||_0<=k} is an infinite union of continuous subspaces. The resulting claim that the projected iterates eventually become constant does not follow, undermining the stationarity proof.

The theoretical algorithm does not match the implemented method. The main method uses a scaled dual variable, stochastic Adam updates, Fisher-weighted projection, and quantized storage of auxiliary variables; Appendix Algorithm 1 instead uses an unscaled multiplier, Euclidean projection, an abstract quantizer, and an inexact-update condition that is neither verified nor enforced in the experiments. Thus, the stated guarantee does not apply to the reported ELSA or ELSA-L procedure.

Even under its assumptions, the theorem only states that any existing limit point is stationary; it neither establishes existence nor convergence of the full iterate sequence. The paper overstates this as convergence to a solution of the original nonconvex problem.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the exact ELSA training-set size and sampling protocol are not reported, code and environment links are blank, several hyperparameter-table entries are missing, and there are no seeds, uncertainty estimates, or tuning-budget details.
ELSA is often worse than established methods at 50–60% sparsity and is not competitive for the evaluated 2:4 and 4:8 patterns. Its advantage is therefore narrower than the broad framing suggests.

The evaluation demonstrates parameter sparsity but not deployment benefit. There are no measurements of inference latency, throughput, energy, or realized memory reduction using sparse kernels, despite practical efficiency being a major motivation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and presents a conceptually appealing shift from sequential layer-wise reconstruction to model-wide optimization of the language-modeling objective.

The unstructured-sparsity results are striking and unusually consistent: across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ELSA substantially improves perplexity over numerous relevant baselines at 80–90% sparsity. The appendix provides the underlying numerical results rather than only plots.

The evaluation extends beyond perplexity to seven zero-shot tasks, multiple architectures, semi-structured and non-uniform sparsity, and a 27B experiment. The objective and projection ablations also support important design choices.
The proposed low-precision state storage is practically motivated, and the paper is generally clear, well organized, and engaging.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not compute- or data-matched. Baselines use 128 calibration sequences, whereas ELSA performs 4,096 full-model optimization steps with batch size 8 and a much larger dataset. There is no comparison against extended-training baselines, ordinary sparse fine-tuning, or prune-and-fine-tune alternatives under equal tokens, FLOPs, and hardware time. Consequently, the evidence does not isolate surrogate-free ADMM as the cause of the gains.

The convergence analysis does not convincingly apply to the implemented method. Objective-aware projection replaces the Euclidean ADMM subproblem with a Fisher-weighted projection, while the stated analysis concerns a different update. Similarly, the ELSA-L algorithm analyzed does not clearly match the practical quantization of both auxiliary states. Most seriously, the proof asserts that the l0-constrained set S is finite, although it is an uncountable union of coordinate subspaces; this invalidates a key subsequence argument as written.

The theory is overstated as convergence to the solution of the constrained problem. The results are conditional statements about limit points being lambda-stationary, under boundedness and inexact-solve assumptions that are not verified experimentally. The scheduled penalty beginning at zero also does not obviously satisfy the theorem's fixed, sufficiently large penalty condition.

Practical efficiency is insufficiently evaluated. The paper reports neither pruning wall-clock time nor total training FLOPs, energy, measured peak memory, inference latency, throughput, or realized sparse-kernel speedups. The claimed 66% memory reduction appears to be state-storage accounting rather than an end-to-end measurement.

Claims that 90% sparsity retains performance without significant degradation are too strong: for LLaMA-2-7B, C4 perplexity rises from 7.26 to 23.14 and average zero-shot accuracy falls from 59.67% to 38.52%. ELSA is nevertheless much better than the tested baselines in this regime.

Results appear to be single runs without uncertainty estimates. ELSA is also weaker than several baselines at moderate sparsity and on 2:4/4:8 sparsity, so its advantage is narrower than some of the broad framing suggests. Overall, the empirical signal is promising, but fair-budget controls and correction or substantial qualification of the theoretical claims are needed for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem and presents a clear model-wide alternative to conventional layer-wise reconstruction-based LLM pruning.

The empirical gains at 80–90% unstructured sparsity are large and consistent across six models spanning several architectures and scales. ELSA establishes substantially better perplexity–parameter trade-offs than the evaluated pruning baselines.

The evaluation is relatively broad: it includes C4 and WikiText perplexity, seven zero-shot tasks, extreme sparsity up to 99%, a 27B model, alternative sparsity patterns, objective/projection ablations, and pruning-cost measurements.
The paper demonstrates that its unstructured sparsity can produce actual memory and generation-throughput improvements using a sparse inference kernel, rather than reporting parameter counts alone.
The objective-aware projection is simple and practically motivated, and the appendix provides useful hyperparameter and numerical-result tables.
weaknesses: The main comparison is substantially confounded by data and optimization budget. ELSA trains on 32,768 length-2048 examples, whereas most headline baselines use only 128 calibration sequences. Equal-data retraining is tested only for Wanda on LLaMA-2-7B, leaving unclear whether ELSA's advantage comes from ADMM specifically or from large-scale task-objective fine-tuning. Strong global sparse-training or iterative pruning/fine-tuning baselines under matched data, steps, and GPU-hours are needed.

The convergence analysis does not appear to cover the implemented method. The practical algorithm uses Adam-based inexact updates, a diagonal Fisher-weighted projection, scheduled penalties, and quantized stored states, while the proof analyzes a different Euclidean projection algorithm with a particular inexactness condition. The paper does not establish that Adam or the stated quantizer satisfies this condition. There are also scaled-versus-unscaled dual-variable inconsistencies and y/z notation errors between the main text and Algorithm 1.

Replacing the Euclidean projection with a Fisher-weighted projection means the z-step no longer minimizes the stated augmented Lagrangian, so the standard ADMM guarantee cannot be transferred directly. Moreover, it is unclear whether Adam's second moment estimates the Fisher of f, since the optimizer is applied to an objective containing the ADMM penalty.

Claims of retaining 'high fidelity' or avoiding significant degradation are overstated. For LLaMA-2-7B at 90% sparsity, C4 perplexity increases from 7.26 to 23.14 and average zero-shot accuracy falls from 59.67% to 38.52%; the 95–99% results degrade further. The deployment gains therefore involve substantial quality loss, and no quality-matched comparison against smaller dense models is provided.

The speed and memory results primarily demonstrate the benefit of the chosen sparsity level and external sparse kernel, not an ELSA-specific systems advantage. They are reported for one model and GPU, without variance, prompt/batch/sequence-length details, or comparisons at matched task quality.

The empirical study reports single values without multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or sensitivity analyses for the penalty schedule and other heavily model- and sparsity-specific hyperparameters. The objective and projection ablations are each narrow and do not isolate all important components.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper says code will be released, but the environment/training-script reference is blank, some table entries are missing, and important details such as optimizer-state handling for the Fisher projection and hyperparameter-search budgets are insufficiently specified.

Overall, the empirical signal is promising and potentially significant, but the unmatched comparisons and disconnect between theory and implementation are major issues. They slightly outweigh the paper's substantial experimental strengths at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem and offers a conceptually sensible alternative to layer-wise reconstruction: jointly optimizing the next-token objective under a global sparsity constraint.

The high-sparsity perplexity improvements are large and consistent across several architectures and model sizes; the LLaMA-2 results also show meaningful downstream accuracy gains over the evaluated pruning baselines.
The evaluation includes practical sparse-kernel latency and memory measurements, a 27B low-precision experiment, compute-cost reporting, and ablations of the objective and projection rule.
The paper is generally well organized, and the appendix provides many numerical results and implementation hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The convergence argument contains a serious mathematical error: the proof asserts that the l0-constrained set S is finite and consequently that a convergent subsequence eventually has constant z iterates. S is an infinite union of continuous subspaces, so this step and the subsequent stationarity conclusion do not follow.

The theory does not cover the method actually emphasized empirically. Algorithm 1 uses ordinary Euclidean projection, whereas ELSA uses the Fisher-weighted objective-aware projection. The assumed approximate x-update condition is also not shown to hold for the finite-step Adam implementation or the stated quantizer. Moreover, the result only characterizes limit points conditionally; it does not establish convergence to a solution as repeatedly claimed.

The main comparison is substantially confounded by training budget. ELSA uses 32,768 sequences, while most pruning baselines use only 128 calibration sequences. The matched-data Wanda+Full baseline freezes a heuristically selected mask and is not an adequate substitute for strong global iterative pruning or sparse continued-pretraining baselines. Thus, the results do not isolate ADMM or the claimed formulation advantage from simply performing much more task-aligned optimization.

Novelty is questionable because ADMM-based pruning, global pruning, iterative retraining, and direct task-loss optimization are established ideas. The paper does not sufficiently position ELSA against compute-matched global sparse-training and gradual-pruning approaches.

The evaluation lacks multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, and a clear hyperparameter-selection protocol despite extensive model- and sparsity-specific tuning. The source-code links are blank, some hyperparameter entries are missing, and key inference-benchmark details are insufficient for reproduction.

Several reported values are internally inconsistent: for example, the main text's OPT-125M and LLaMA-2-13B perplexities do not match Table 10. These discrepancies weaken confidence in the empirical record.

Claims of retaining high model fidelity are overstated. At 90% sparsity, LLaMA-2-7B average accuracy falls from 59.67 to 38.52 and C4 perplexity more than triples; the 95–99% results report only perplexity. Efficiency gains are therefore not demonstrated at matched model quality.

ELSA is often inferior at moderate sparsity and is merely comparable or worse under deployable N:M sparsity, so the contribution is narrower than the broad framing suggests. Overall, the striking high-sparsity results are promising, but the invalid theoretical justification and insufficiently controlled evaluation prevent acceptance in the present form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and offers a clear contribution: globally optimizing the language-modeling objective under a sparsity constraint instead of relying on sequential layer-wise reconstruction surrogates.

The empirical gains at high sparsity are unusually large and consistent. Across six model configurations from 125M to 13B parameters, ELSA substantially improves perplexity at 70–90% sparsity, with corresponding gains in downstream zero-shot accuracy.

The evaluation is broad, covering multiple architectures and scales, sparsity levels up to 99%, seven downstream tasks, alternative sparsity patterns, a 27B low-precision variant, and objective/projection ablations.
The paper demonstrates that the sparsity gains produce real deployment benefits using a sparse inference kernel, including up to 3.98x throughput and 7.80x memory improvement.
The matched-data Wanda plus full-fine-tuning comparison provides useful evidence that ELSA's advantage is not explained solely by performing additional training.
The presentation is generally clear, well motivated, and supported by detailed numerical tables and implementation settings.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are not fully compute- or data-matched: ELSA uses 32,768 training sequences and iterative optimization, whereas most pruning baselines use only 128 calibration sequences. The matched-budget retraining comparison is limited to one model and does not include stronger global iterative-pruning or projected-gradient baselines across the main evaluation grid.

The convergence analysis appears materially flawed or, at minimum, incomplete. The proof explicitly claims that the l0-constrained set S is finite, although it contains infinitely many real-valued vectors; this invalidates the step asserting that projected iterates become constant along a subsequence.

The theoretical algorithm does not cleanly match the practical method. The analysis uses Euclidean projection and an ambiguously specified quantized update, while the implemented method uses Fisher-weighted projection and quantized auxiliary states. Consequently, the stated guarantee does not evidently apply to the full ELSA/ELSA-L procedure evaluated experimentally.

The paper overstates its theorem as convergence to a solution of the constrained problem. The result is conditional on bounded iterates and the existence of a limit point and establishes only stationarity of limit points, not global optimality or convergence of the complete sequence.

Some reported values in the main text disagree with the appendix tables—for example, the OPT-125M and LLaMA-2-13B perplexities quoted in Section 5.1 differ from Table 10—raising quality-control concerns.

Reproducibility is only moderate: source code is promised rather than supplied in the manuscript, several per-model hyperparameter entries are unclear or missing, and the computational cost of broad hyperparameter selection is not reported. Statistical variation across training runs is also absent.

The method is much less competitive at moderate or semi-structured sparsity, sometimes trailing existing methods. Its practical impact therefore depends on hardware and kernels that can efficiently exploit highly unstructured sparsity.
